Look for the donation box when you shop at Sunnyside and help us make a difference with your support.
What is SEED?

SEED is the acronym for the Social Equity and Educational Development Initiative at  Cresco Labs. SEED’s mission is to develop tangible pathways into the cannabis industry for communities impacted by the War on Drugs through our three pillars: restorative justice, community business incubation, and education & workforce development.
SEED’s vision is realized through its three pillars:
Restorative Justice
SEED commits to elevating people whose lives have been impacted by the War on Drugs by working to remedy those harms.

SEED’s restorative justice programming includes expungement events, lobbying to progress and change the nation's drug laws, and working to ensure that no person remains in prison for a cannabis conviction.
Community Business Incubator
The Community Business Incubator is designed to empower and jumpstart the creation of minority-owned cannabis businesses.
SEED provides both the technical and financial assistance necessary to apply, open and operate a cannabis business.
Education and Workforce Development

SEED’s Education and Workforce Development Pillar develops cannabis programming tailored to communities disproportionately impacted by the War on Drugs. This curriculum was designed to help individuals develop the skills needed to strategically and successfully enter the cannabis industry.
SEED builds collaborative relationships with colleges and universities to develop coursework to educate and prepare students for careers in the growing cannabis industry.
Here's a deeper look into the organizations we're supporting this Black History Month:
Cabrini Green Legal Aid

Cabrini Green Legal Aid has become a national leader in supporting low-income individuals negatively impacted by the criminal justice system. CGLA gives justice a voice through collaboration, innovation, and collective impact.
Institute for Community Justice

ICJ provides individuals impacted by mass incarceration with support services that empower them to thrive as their fullest selves. As tireless advocates for equitable access to healthcare, safety, and justice, ICJ envisions a world free from mass incarceration–where individuals have the opportunity to design their freedom.
New York Urban League

For the past 100 years, NYUL’s mission has been to strengthen underserved communities through education, employment, empowerment and advocacy - in order to ensure every community’s collective voice is heard.

Join us in celebrating the stories and contributions of a few of our Black team members, as they share their journeys within the cannabis industry. It's also important to understand and reflect on how we got to where we are today, with regards to cannabis, its use, and its future. We'll take a look at cannabis's journey westward, the role it played in the 1900s America, and how it can shape opportunities for future generations.
The Arrival of Cannabis in Africa

Cannabis has origins throughout the African continent, particularly in the Sub-Saharan portion (1). In more Northern regions, Cannabis was introduced to Africa by way of Arabian merchants in the 1200s, who brought it over from the Middle East and Asia (1). By the 1800s, the British were using indentured servants from India in the Caribbean for labor on rubber and sugar plantations, and they brought cannabis along with them (2). This created an environment where Indian and Jamaican cultures began folding cannabis into their own communities, becoming especially popular with youth workers. In 1833, slavery was outlawed in Britain and its colonies and the plantations in Jamaica and Barbados could no longer hold the servants against their will. This allowed those newly liberated plantation workers to move, settling in Jamaica and the American South, growing the popularity of cannabis in those areas.
Cannabis and Black America

Cannabis entered the United States through Caribbean sailors and immigrants as well as those fleeing the aftermath of the Mexican Revolution of 1910 (3, 4). As a result, Black and Brown communities began using cannabis recreationally more commonly, especially since it was not new to Black Americans, whose parents and grandparents would have been introduced to the plant while enslaved on hemp plantations (5). One group that put cannabis on the map for its creative effects was the jazz community, particularly Black jazz musicians. Its social and creative aspects played a role in the works of iconic, timeless musicians like Duke Ellington and Louis Armstrong. There were also those who wanted to entirely remove cannabis from American society. When Henry Anslinger was made the director of the Federal Bureau of Narcotics, the organization responsible before US Drug Enforcement Administration, he began leading the charge to federally ban cannabis by the 1930s (6). Propaganda was widely distributed, promoting racist narratives associating Black and Brown people with cannabis use and criminality. Then, with the passing of the Marijuana Tax Act in 1937, the distribution, possession, and use of cannabis became effectively illegal and highly punishable (7). With that foundation of fear-mongering and bigoted rhetoric set, Anslinger attacked cannabis and jazz - an almost entirely Black culture. Fast-forward to the Nixon Administration and the seeds had been sown for America to begin its full-on the War on Drugs, disproportionality policing cannabis and other drugs in Black communities (8).
Modern Times

Unfortunately, we still see aspects of the past in the present, despite the progress we've made as a nation. According to a recent study done by the ACLU, Black people are 3.73 times more likely to be arrested for a cannabis-related crime than their white counterparts, even though usage is roughly equal across races (9). As a result, we're continuing our work to provide more avenues and opportunities for Black communities to profit from the expansion of the cannabis industry. We're proud to work with organizations on advocacy, education, and promoting equity within the cannabis industry for Black individuals and communities. We'd like to shine a light on the following: Minority Cannabis Business Association (MCBA) The National Black Farmers Association (NBA) The National Cannabis Industry Association (NCIA)
Black History Month at Sunnyside

As a part of Black History Month, we are excited to honor and celebrate the contributions of our team members from the Black community. As part of this cultural moment, we'll be featuring employee spotlights that highlight your stories, your connection to cannabis, and the impact they're making in our dispensaries and community We asked them: How do you think Black History has played a role in your life and did it inspire you to pursue a career in cannabis? What do you think the future looks like for Black communities and voices within the cannabis space? Is there any intersection of Black History and the history of cannabis that you find particularly interesting? What initiatives or changes would you like to see in the cannabis industry to better support and include Black communities and voices? We'd like to share some of the responses with you here, as a way of both championing our own team members as well as educating on what more we can do as an industry.

data.text: How do you think Black History has played a role in your life and did it inspire you to pursue a career in cannabis? Black History itself has educated me on my roots and the cultural impact in America. I wouldn't say it inspired me career-wise, more so the diversity of my hometown New Kensington. What do you think the future looks like for Black communities and voices within the cannabis space? My hope is that more states go 100% recreational so more opportunities are open to the low-income or middle class. Black/POC representation and ownership in the cannabis industry is extremely low in comparison. Is there any intersection of Black History and the history of cannabis that you find particularly interesting? The stigma of cannabis as a drug when "Reefer Madness" came out and targeted African Americans and other POC. Prior to that cannabis was used in OTC Medicinals like cough syrup. The racism around cannabis is deep-rooted and I can only hope we make a difference. What initiatives or changes would you like to see in the cannabis industry to better support and include Black communities and voices? More representation and diversity all around.

data.alt: Terrell: Dispensary Manager at Sunnyside Philadelphia

data.text: How do you think Black History has played a role in your life and did it inspire you to pursue a career in cannabis? Growing up as a Black man in South Philadelphia, l've seen firsthand the impact of systemic inequality and racism on our communities. Black history, in particular, has played a significant role in shaping my life and career choices. Seeing the struggles and triumphs of Black leaders and activists throughout history, from Frederick Douglass to Martin Luther King Jr., has instilled in me a sense of pride, resilience, and determination. Their stories taught me the importance of perseverance, community, and fighting for justice. Now, as a Dispensary Manager in the cannabis industry, I recognize the significance of Black history in shaping my career path. The War on Drugs, which disproportionately affected Black communities, has had a lasting impact on our society. The cannabis industry, in particular, has a complex and problematic history regarding racial equity. However, I see my role in the cannabis industry as an opportunity to help rectify some of the past injustices. By working in this field, I aim to promote equity, inclusion, and social justice. I'm committed to ensuring that our dispensary serves as a positive force in the community, providing education, jobs, and access to cannabis for those who need it. Black history has inspired me to pursue a career in cannabis because I believe that our community deserves a seat at the table. I'm proud to be part of a growing movement that seeks to address the racial disparities in the cannabis industry and promote a more equitable future. What do you think the future looks like for Black communities and voices within the cannabis space? As a Black man from South Philadelphia working in the cannabis industry, I'm optimistic about the future of the Black community and voices within the cannabis space. Here's what I envision: Increased Representation and Ownership: More Black-owned dispensaries, grow operations, and cannabis-related businesses will emerge, creating economic opportunities and wealth within our communities. Amplified Voices and Advocacy: Black voices will continue to gain prominence in shaping cannabis policies, laws, and industry practices. Advocates will push for greater equity, justice, and access, ensuring that our communities benefit from the growing cannabis economy. Community-Focused Initiatives: Cannabis companies will prioritize community investment, partnering with organizations to create jobs, provide education, and support social justice initiatives. This will help address the historical harm inflicted upon Black communities by the War on Drugs. Education and Awareness: Efforts to educate Black communities about the benefits and risks of cannabis will increase, addressing the lingering effects of prohibition-era propaganda. This will empower individuals to make informed decisions about their health and wellness. Policy Reforms and Expungement: Advocacy efforts will lead to continued policy reforms, including expungement of cannabis-related offenses, releasing individuals from the grip of the criminal justice system. This will help rebuild lives and communities damaged by the War on Drugs. Black Culture and Excellence: The cannabis industry will acknowledge and celebrate Black culture's contributions to the plant's history, music, art, and social justice movements. This recognition will help foster a more inclusive and equitable industry. The future of the Black community and voices within the cannabis space is bright. As we continue to push for equity, justice, and access, l'm confident that our communities will thrive and become leaders in the cannabis industry. Is there any intersection of Black History and the history of cannabis that you find particularly interesting? Yes, there's a significant intersection of Black history and the history of cannabis that I find particularly interesting. The Origins of Cannabis Prohibition: Cannabis was initially introduced to the United States by enslaved Africans, who brought their knowledge of the plant's medicinal and spiritual properties. However, as cannabis use became more widespread, racist and xenophobic attitudes towards African Americans, Latinos, and Asian Americans fueled the push for prohibition. The Role of Harry Anslinger: Harry Anslinger, the first commissioner of the Federal Bureau of Narcotics, played a pivotal role in the prohibition of cannabis. Anslinger was known for his racist views and used propaganda to link cannabis use to African Americans and Mexicans, further stigmatizing the plant. The Impact on Black Communities: The War on Drugs, which began in the 1970s, disproportionately targeted Black communities, leading to mass incarceration, police brutality, and systemic inequality. This legacy of oppression continues to affect Black communities today. The Connection to Jazz and Music: Cannabis has a rich history in Black music, particularly in the jazz scene of the 1920s and 1930s. Many famous jazz musicians, such as Louis Armstrong and Duke Ellington, used cannabis for creative inspiration and relaxation. The Modern-Day Impact: Today, as the cannabis industry grows, it's essential to acknowledge the historical injustices inflicted upon Black communities. Many advocates are pushing for equity and inclusion in the industry, including expungement of cannabis-related offenses, community reinvestment, and increased representation of Black-owned businesses. This intersection of Black history and cannabis history highlights the need for restorative justice, equity, and inclusion in the cannabis industry. What initiatives or changes would you like to see in the cannabis industry to better support and include Black communities and voices? As a Black man from South Philadelphia working in the cannabis industry, I've got some strong thoughts on this. Here are some initiatives and changes I'd like to see: Equity and Inclusion:
1. ﻿Increased Black ownership and representation: More Black-owned dispensaries, grow operations, and cannabis-related businesses are essential.
﻿﻿﻿2. Diverse hiring practices: Cannabis companies should prioritize hiring Black candidates, especially in leadership positions.
3. ﻿﻿﻿Internships and training programs: Provide opportunities for Black individuals to gain experience and skills in the cannabis industry.
Community Investment:
1. Reinvestment in Black communities: Cannabis companies should invest in community development projects, such as education, job training, and healthcare initiatives.
2. Expungement and record-clearing: Support efforts to expunge cannabis-related offenses and clear records, helping individuals rebuild their lives.
3. Community outreach and education: Provide cannabis education and awareness programs in Black communities, addressing health disparities and promoting responsible use.
Policy Reforms:
1. Social equity licensing: Implement licensing programs that prioritize Black applicants and promote equity in the industry.
2. Cannabis decriminalization and legalization: Advocate for federal decriminalization and legalization, addressing the War on Drugs' legacy.
3. Regulatory reform: Simplify and streamline regulations to reduce barriers to entry for Black entrepreneurs.
Cultural Sensitivity and Awareness:
1. Cultural competency training: Provide training for cannabis industry professionals to understand and address the unique needs and concerns of Black communities.
2. Inclusive marketing and branding: Ensure marketing and branding efforts are inclusive and respectful of Black culture.

3. Celebrating Black cannabis culture: Acknowledge and celebrate the contributions of Black culture to the cannabis industry. These initiatives and changes will help create a more equitable and inclusive cannabis industry, addressing the historical injustices faced by Black communities.

data.text: It's a great day for U.S. cannabis! The decision to move cannabis from a Schedule I to a Schedule III substance acknowledges what millions of Americans already know: cannabis is medicine and deserves responsible, common-sense regulation. Under the Controlled Substances Act, this action recognizes cannabis's medicinal value, providing more access to research and education. Rescheduling starts bridging the gap between federal law and the will of Americans, with nearly 90% of our nation supporting some form of cannabis legalization and 74% already living in states with legal cannabis. It also opens the door to deeper medical research, giving scientists the freedom to study this special plant that humans have turned to for more than 5,000 years. For the millions of people who use cannabis to help manage pain, find calm, or simply enjoy life, this moment is long overdue. Let's soak it up. 🧡

What kinds of products will I find?
Flower

Flower is the most common form of cannabis and our most popular product. It’s sold as loose buds that are commonly smoked or vaporized. Typically, flower is sold in three varieties: fuller-sized buds, popcorn buds that are smaller in size, and shake–which is loose flower. Another convenient way to buy flower is as a pre-rolled joint (or a smaller shortie) that comes ready to smoke.
Vapes

Vapes are a popular way to consume cannabis simply and discreetly. Vapes are pre-filled vaporizer cartridges or pods. These small, battery-powered devices come preloaded with cannabis oil and allow you to enjoy at the push of a button.

Flower

Flower is the most common form of medical marijuana and our most popular product. It’s sold as loose buds that are commonly smoked or vaporized. Typically, flower is sold in three varieties: fuller-sized buds, popcorn buds that are smaller in size, and shake–which is loose flower.
Vapes

Vapes are a popular way to consume medical marijuana simply and discreetly. Vapes are pre-filled vaporizer cartridges or pods. These small, battery-powered devices come preloaded with medical marijuana oil and allow you to enjoy at the push of a button.

Topicals

Topicals are products like creams and lotions that come infused with medical marijuana and are applied directly to your skin. They are a great option for sore muscles, inflammation, and localized pain management. When medical marijuana is applied to the skin it does not typically have the same intoxicating, psychoactive effects you might expect when smoking, vaporizing, or eating the plant.

title: Drive thru Dispensary Pickup in Florida

data.text: Streamlined to save you time.

We’re giving you more options when it comes to shopping for cannabis. Visit us in-store, place your order online, or use our brand-new drive thru lane for pick-up at our Ocala, Fern Park, Port St. Lucie, Sarasota, Orlando - South, Cape Coral, Palm Harbor, Lady Lake, Miami - West, Avon Park, and Destin locations. Whichever path you pick, we'll make it easy for you.
Here's how it works:
1. Order online.
Browse our live menu and submit your order. You'll need to place an online order to use our new drive-thru service.
2. Get your order.
Pick up your order in-store, or use our new Drive Thru! We accept cash, debit, and CanPay at Drive Thru. You'll need to bring your medical card.
Get to know the traffic flow.

Drive-thru pick-up service is available at our Ocala, Fern Park, Port St. Lucie, Sarasota, Orlando - South, Cape Coral, Palm Harbor, Lady Lake, Miami - West,  Avon Park, and Destin locations; with more to come!
Need something more? Come shop with us in-store.

If you need more help choosing the right products or if drive thru just isn’t your thing, you can also opt to shop inside the dispensary. If you'd like to change your online order, please visit us in-store. We look forward to seeing you!
Have questions? Ask us anything!
Check out our FAQ or drop us a line.
Delivery
Where do you deliver?
Delivery is currently available in Florida. Enter your zip code here to see if you're located within our delivery zone.
How long does it take to receive a delivery?
Orders placed Monday through Saturday after 7pm will be reviewed, accepted, and scheduled on the following day (pending availability). Holiday delivery hours may vary—see details at checkout.
How does delivery work?

We deliver Monday through Saturday—we do not deliver on Sunday. Orders placed Monday through Saturday after 7pm will be reviewed, accepted, and scheduled on the following day (pending availability). Once your order is placed, you'll receive an email or text confirmation that your order has been received. A scheduling agent will call you to confirm that the order has been accepted for delivery. Please be on the lookout for the call to avoid scheduling delays. If we aren’t able to reach you, our team will leave a voicemail at the phone number you provided.
Is there a delivery fee?
Delivery is free on orders of $75 or more (after discounts), at all locations. For orders under these minimums, we charge a delivery fee that will show up when you checkout.
I placed a delivery order, but decided to come pick it up instead. What should I do?
If you would like to cancel a delivery order, you can do this by visiting your account page, or by giving us a call.
Pricing & Promotions
Do you have a loyalty program?
Yes, we do! Click here to learn more.
What if I apply loyalty points and then cancel my order?
Worry not! Online rewards redemptions that aren’t applied in-store at the register will be returned to your Sunnyside account. This will reflect on your account within 48-72 hours.
What happened to 'Buy More, Save More' pricing?

We recently lowered pricing on flower, concentrates, and tinctures. We are constantly evaluating pricing against our peers to ensure you get the highest quality products at a fair and competitive price. We will also offer specials and promotions on some of our best-selling items—you can view our current promotions and real-time inventory here .
Do you offer Birthday discounts?

Yes, we offer a 25% off discounts for your special day, at all Florida locations! Please visit us in-store to redeem. Limit one use per year. Not valid with other offers. Must be redeemed within your birthday month.
Do you offer Veterans' Discounts?

Yes, all retired or active service members and their spouses can receive a 25% off discount, which can be redeemed in-store. Just show your DD214 or an ID that reflects your or your spouse's veteran status, and your discount will be applied when you pick up your order at the dispensary. Not valid with other offers.
Do you offer new patient discounts?

New patients receive 25% off their first order! If you've already used this discount at a One Plant dispensary, you cannot use it again at our new Sunnyside locations in Florida. Discount will be applied in-store and must be redeemed by your 2nd visit. Not valid with other offers.
How can I find out about new deals or promotions?

We are always rolling out new offers for our customers. Be sure to sign up for text or email updates here to learn about deals, events, shop updates and more. You can also check out our Promos & Deals page to see current specials.
Store Information
Are minors allowed inside the dispensary?
Minors are allowed into the store when accompanied by their caretaker or guardian, who must be over the age of 18.
What can I use as a valid ID?
You'll need a non-expired government issued ID such as a license, state ID, or passport. Your ID must include a photo, date of birth, and a visible expiration date.
Do customers need to present a medical card and a state ID to shop?

Indeed they do; patients and their caregivers must have an active Medical Marijuana Use Registry Identification Card with a Valid ID. Your Department of Health approval letter may be used while your ID is being issued. Have a question? Reach out to our customer service team.
How do I get a medical card?
It's easy to register for a Medical Marijuana Card. Read our handy guide here .
Do I need to designate one dispensary?
Nope, Florida medical patients can shop more than one dispensary—and we encourage you to explore.
Are pets allowed in the dispensary?
Registered or identified service animals are allowed inside of our dispensaries while shopping.
What forms of payment do you take?
We accept debit cards, CanPay, and cash. We also have ATMs located in every store for your convenience.
What is your cell phone policy?
You can use your phone in our dispensary, but photo and video are prohibited, although we’re flattered. Please be mindful of the privacy of others while in our stores.
Online Ordering
How do I place an online order?

Ordering online is easy at Sunnyside. If it’s your first time, you’ll need to register with us first. Then select your store and customer type, then add products to your cart from our real-time inventory. Once you’re done, hit submit and you’re all set! We’ll shoot you an email or text confirming that we’ve received your order. Click here to register for an account.
Why am I unable to place an order?
We may be experiencing high demand. Please contact us to place an order over the phone.
Can I return or exchange a defective product at Sunnyside?

Due to the nature of medical marijuana products, all sales are final. If you're having an issue with a defective product, please reach out to us here and a member of our Customer Care team will assist you as soon as possible.
Cannabis Questions
Can I travel with cannabis?
Since cannabis is not legal at the federal level, you cannot take product outside of the state in which it was purchased.
What different forms of cannabis are there?

These days, cannabis comes in a wide variety of formats to better fit a wider variety of lifestyles. Flower (dried and cured cannabis buds) may still be the most popular form out there, but alternatives like edibles, vapes and topicals can offer you different experiences. Check out our article on Basic Forms of Cannabis to learn more.
What are some common ways to use cannabis?

There are lots of different ways to consume cannabis, such as smoking, vaping or eating it. Each has its advantages, depending on the effect you’re after. To learn more about all your options, check out our article on Common Ways to Consume Cannabis .
What are THC and CBD?

These two three-letter acronyms are key to unlocking the world of cannabis. Knowing what they mean will help you make the most of your cannabis experience. It’s good knowledge to have before you start shopping for cannabis. You can read our full article to learn more about THC and CBD here .
Are there smoke-free cannabis options?

Edibles are a great option for those who would like to try cannabis but aren’t fans of smoke. Everything from gummies to edibles to chocolates to chews to beverages—all kinds of ways to enjoy cannabis, smoke-free style. Just know that edible products take effect differently than products you inhale. Check out our Intro to Edibles article to learn more.
What are indica and sativa?

Maybe you’ve seen these terms before, but what they mean can tell you about the cannabis you’re enjoying. Check out our article on Indica vs. Sativa to learn more about these common cannabis strain types.

One Plant
Transition Questions
Is One Plant going away?

No, One Plant will continue to make hand-trimmed, high-quality cannabis products in the state of Florida. Sunnyside will continue to sell One Plant products. Plus, we will have exciting new products coming soon- stay tuned!
When is the change happening?
All One Plant Dispensaries are now Sunnyside!
Will I need to create a new account on Sunnyside.shop?
Yes, we make the process quick and easy from start to finish. Here's how to create an account and place your first online order.
Still have questions?

This April, we're still learning how to live apart, yet remain connected. The concept of "420" has always been a communal event—this year just requires a bit more ingenuity to safely carry on that tradition. Here's some inspiration to get you started:
Micro Mornings

Rise and shine–it's micro time! Microdosing, as the name implies, means consuming a very small amount to feel more focused or creative rather than high. Low-dosed products that have a balance of CBD and THC offer an approachable way to start the day.
Afternoon Stroll

Nature walks and marijuana were made for each other. Consume at home and then take a walk with someone you live with or a nature-loving dog for some fresh air. Convenient, mini pre-rolled joints (Shorties) are a simple way to heighten your senses.
Long Distance Puff/Pass

Video chat with close friends or family members while enjoying a little puff or two off a vape pen or pre-roll. Smoking shareable forms solo helps it feel like a real-life session. Amazing what sharing laughs with familiar faces can do for the soul.
Get Baking
Spark creativity in the kitchen with some sativa flower. Summon your chef skills and treat yourself by baking a batch of brownies or cookies from scratch. Your home will smell incredible!
Late Night Screening
Indulge in a delicious edible and cue up some cannabis-friendly content such as stand-up comedians, funny movies or a sitcom marathon featuring a series you love.

Like with trips to the grocery store or takeout, and just about everything else — wash hands well after any outside interactions.
3. Start low and go slow.
Especially with edibles, give yourself an hour or so to settle into it before taking more than the minimum recommended dose.
4. Don't puff and pass.
These days, it's best practice to keep anything that hits your lips to yourself.
5. Enjoy the ride.
For this moment anyways, turn down the news, relinquish any tendency to tackle all the world's problems and focus on simple things that can bring you joy.

How do I print or save my active medical card on my phone?
1. Log into the state website here
2. Find your active registration under the 'Tracking Inbox' section at the top of the screen.
3. Select "Print Card"
4. If you're on an iPhone, you can click the share icon at the bottom of your screen, and select 'Save to Files'.
How much medical marijuana can you buy in Illinois?
The limit is up to 2.5 ounces within a 14-day period. Although you may ask your doctor to submit a waiver/exception to get that limit increased.
How many dispensaries can I visit in one day with an Illinois Medical Marijuana Card?
As many as you want! However, note that each dispensary will have a record of your daily purchase and won't exceed the state-mandated limit of 2.5 ozs within a two-week period.

Illinois medical customers can shop at any of Sunnyside Dispensaries' 5 dual-use (medical and recreational) locations: Wrigleyville/Lakeview, Champaign, Elmwood Park, Rockford, and Buffalo Grove. Click here to see a full list of our Illinois dispensaries.
How can I renew or extend my Illinois Medical Marijuana Card?

If you didn't buy a 3-year card, you can apply for an extension renewal for up to 3 years. You'll need to pay the fee again—but you won't need to get another certification from your doctor. If you've had your card for 3 years or if it's expired—you'll need to get another doctor certification. BUT if you asked your doctor for a 'lifelong certification' and they granted the request, you won't need a new doctor certification—as long as you renewed your medical card before it expired. Sure! Visit any Sunnyside medical or dual-use dispensary and we'll show you how to apply.

Can I enter a medical dispensary without a medical card in Illinois?

Any adult (21+) in Illinois can buy legal cannabis at an adult-use or dual-use dispensary as a recreational customer. If you'd like to purchase medical marijuana, you'll need to present your medical card at a dispensary that serves medical/dual-use customers.

What kinds of products will I find?
Flower

Flower is the most common form of cannabis and our most popular product. It’s sold as loose buds that are commonly smoked or vaporized. Typically, flower is sold in three varieties: fuller-sized buds, popcorn buds that are smaller in size, and shake–which is loose flower. Another convenient way to buy flower is as a pre-rolled joint (or a smaller shortie) that comes ready to smoke.
Edibles

Edibles are the ideal smoke-free alternative for anyone from beginners to more experienced users. Infused gummies, snacks or drinks make incorporating cannabis into an active lifestyle and wellness routine simple. Keep in mind, eating cannabis offers a different experience than smoking or vaping. 
When it comes to edibles, it’s best to start low and go slow before you know how your body will react. Eat one, then wait 1-2 hours to allow for the onset before considering taking another. Here’s our guide to safely experimenting with edibles.
Vapes

Vapes are a popular way to consume cannabis simply and discreetly. Vapes are pre-filled vaporizer cartridges or pods. These small, battery-powered devices come preloaded with cannabis oil and allow you to enjoy at the push of a button.
Tinctures

Tinctures are liquid cannabis elixirs that are taken orally, sublingually or simply added to food and drinks. Tinctures are a common form of cannabis medicine. They're discreet and make dosing as easy as just adding a drop or two. Their effects are quickly noticed, often felt within minutes.
Easy to dose, these tinctures are available in a variety of formulations of THC & CBD to meet a variety of wellness needs. Learn more about how THC and CBD work differently in your body.
Topicals

Topicals are products like creams and lotions that come infused with cannabis and are applied directly to your skin. They are a great option for sore muscles, inflammation, and localized pain management. When cannabis is applied to the skin it does not typically have the same intoxicating, psychoactive effects you might expect when smoking, vaporizing, or eating the plant.
Concentrates

Cannabis concentrates (products like extracts, oil, and hash), are created by concentrating the resinous oils extracted from cannabis plants. These oils are distilled into concentrates that deliver the full flavor profile and the potency of the flower. Concentrates offer all the enjoyable aspects of cannabis, without having to burn the plant.

Frequently Asked Questions:
How much does it cost to get an Illinois Medical Marijuana Card?

$50 for 1 year, $100 for 2 years, or $125 for 3 years. You may also apply as a 'reduced fee applicant' if you're a Veteran or receive Supplemental Security Income (SSI) or Social Security Disability Income (SSDI). The reduced fees for a medical marijuana card in the State of Illinois are $25 for 1 year, $50 for 2 years, and $75 for 3 years. To qualify, you'll need to upload a copy of your Social Security Benefit Verification statements or alternatively, a copy of Veteran Form DD-214.
How do I find a doctor who can get me certified for a Medical Marijuana Card in Illinois?

Try contacting the recommended doctors above, or ask your primary care physician if they're certified to provide a medical cannabis recommendation. You may also request that your doctor provide you with a 'lifelong certification', which is at their discretion—but will allow you to keep renewing your card without a new doctor certification, as long as you don't let your card expire.
If I haven't completed my application yet, can a doctor certification expire?

If you haven't completed your application yet, a pending doctor certification will only remain eligible for 90 days from the date of the exam. So you'll need your doctor to certify you within 3 months of your application.
Are there any required documents?
Yes. You'll need to submit:
Government-issued ID (Current Illinois driver’s license or state ID)

items: A current, valid, government-issued ID, such as an Illinois Drivers License or State ID

A 2″x2″ color photo (similar to a passport photo), taken within the last 30 days, on a solid-colored background, with just you alone in the frame. While you can try this on an iPhone, it might be easier to visit a pharmacy or local passport photo service.
To prove Illinois residency, you might be required to submit a voter ID card, a bank statement, or utility bills.
If you're applying with a caregiver, you'll need that caregiver's identification.
If you're applying as a 'reduced fee applicant', you'll need to submit Social Security Benefit Verification statements or alternatively, a copy of Veteran Form DD-214.

data.text: How long will it take to receive my Illinois Medical Marijuana card?

If you apply online and get approved, a temporary (provisional registry) card will be sent to you via email within 24 hours of completing your online application. You can also log into the MCPP website here , select ' Print Provisional Registration' , and you can visit a dispensary the same-day. Note: the state no longer prints physical cards, so once your application is fully approved, you'll need to log in to your account and either print your card or save the PDF to your phone. As long as you present a physical copy or a digital version of your card at the dispensary door, you'll be able to shop as a medical customer. For more information, click here or call 855-636-3688 .
How do I print or save my active medical card on my phone?
1. Log into the state website here
2. Find your active registration under the 'Tracking Inbox' section at the top of the screen.
3. Select "Print Card"
4. If you're on an iPhone, you can click the share icon at the bottom of your screen, and select 'Save to Files'.
How much medical marijuana can you buy in Illinois?
The limit is up to 2.5 ounces within a 14-day period. Although you may ask your doctor to submit a waiver/exception to get that limit increased.
How many dispensaries can I visit in one day with an Illinois Medical Marijuana Card?
As many as you want! However, note that each dispensary will have a record of your daily purchase and won't exceed the state-mandated limit of 2.5 ozs within a two-week period.
Where can I buy legal medical marijuana in Illinois?

Illinois medical customers can shop at any of Sunnyside Dispensaries' 5 dual-use (medical and recreational) locations: Wrigleyville/Lakeview, Champaign, Elmwood Park, Rockford, and Buffalo Grove. Click here to see a full list of our Illinois dispensaries.
How can I renew or extend my Illinois Medical Marijuana Card?

If you didn't buy a 3-year card, you can apply for an extension renewal for up to 3 years. You'll need to pay the fee again—but you won't need to get another certification from your doctor. If you've had your card for 3 years or if it's expired—you'll need to get another doctor certification. BUT if you asked your doctor for a 'lifelong certification' and they granted the request, you won't need a new doctor certification—as long as you renewed your medical card before it expired. Note that the IDPH (Illinois Department of Public Health), will notify you via email of an impending medical card expiration.
Can you help me understand how to get a medical card?
Sure! Visit any Sunnyside medical or dual-use dispensary and we'll show you how to apply.
Does the State of Illinois still send physical cards via mail?

No, the IDPH stopped printing physical cards during COVID. You can either print out a card from their website, or download a PDF version to your phone. Either form is acceptable when entering a medical or dual-use dispensary.
Can I enter a medical dispensary without a medical card in Illinois?

Any adult (21+) in Illinois can buy legal cannabis at an adult-use or dual-use dispensary as a recreational customer. If you'd like to purchase medical marijuana, you'll need to present your medical card at a dispensary that serves medical/dual-use customers.
Can I get a Medical Marijuana Card in Illinois if I'm under 18?

Yes, if you can prove Illinois residency, you'll need to specify an adult caregiver and provide doctor certifications from two distinct physicians. The fees for caregivers are  $25 for 1 year, $50 for 2 years, and $75 for 3 years. You can specify up to 3 caregivers who may order and pick up medical marijuana for you. For each extra caregiver, you'll need to pay $25.
Do I still need to select a 'preferred dispensary'?

No! The great news is Illinois Medical patients no longer need to designate a specific dispensary on their application. You can visit any Illinois medical marijuana dispensary. But if you enter a recreational-only dispensary, you won't be able to receive your tax discounts.
What about the Opioid Alternative Pilot Program (OAPP)?
Illinois residents 21+ who have (or could have) been prescribed opioid medications due to a medical condition may qualify. Click here to learn more.

What kinds of products will I find?
Flower

Flower is the most common form of cannabis and our most popular product. It’s sold as loose buds that are commonly smoked or vaporized. data.text: Vapes

Vapes are a popular way to consume cannabis simply and discreetly. Vapes are pre-filled vaporizer cartridges or pods. These small, battery-powered devices come preloaded with cannabis oil and allow you to enjoy at the push of a button.

data.alt: Liquid Live Resin cannabis extract flowing from marijuana flower into a vape cartridge

data.text: Edibles

Edibles are the ideal smoke-free alternative for anyone from beginners to more experienced users. Infused gummies, snacks or drinks make incorporating cannabis into an active lifestyle and wellness routine simple. Keep in mind, eating cannabis offers a different experience than smoking or vaping.

When it comes to edibles, it’s best to start low and go slow before you know how your body will react. Eat one, then wait 1-2 hours to allow for the onset before considering taking another. Here’s our guide to safely experimenting with edibles.

data.alt: Sliced mango next to pieces of mango marijuana edibles

data.text: Tinctures

Tinctures are liquid cannabis elixirs that are taken orally, sublingually or simply added to food and drinks. Tinctures are a common form of cannabis medicine. They're discreet and make dosing as easy as just adding a drop or two. Their effects are quickly noticed, often felt within minutes. Easy to dose, these tinctures are available in a variety of formulations of THC & CBD to meet a variety of wellness needs. Learn more about how THC and CBD work differently in your body.

data.alt: Hand holding a bottle of Remedi cannabis tincture with a half filled dropper above it in front of white flowers

data.text: Topicals

Topicals are products like creams and lotions that come infused with cannabis and are applied directly to your skin. They are a great option for sore muscles, inflammation, and localized pain management. When cannabis is applied to the skin it does not typically have the same intoxicating, psychoactive effects you might expect when smoking, vaporizing, or eating the plant.

data.alt: Hand applying cannabis topicals to upper arm

data.text: Concentrates

Cannabis concentrates (products like extracts, oil, and hash), are created by concentrating the resinous oils extracted from cannabis plants. These oils are distilled into concentrates that deliver the full flavor profile and the potency of the flower. Concentrates offer all the enjoyable aspects of cannabis, without having to burn the plant.

What is Sunnyside?

Sunnyside is your go-to destination in Illinois for adult-use and medical cannabis, cannabis education , and support. We’re more than just a dispensary — we’re here to help you explore cannabis comfortably, confidently, and judgment-free.

Anyone 21 or older with a valid government-issued ID can purchase adult-use cannabis in Illinois. No medical card is required for adult-use customers.

Yes! Many of our Illinois locations serve both medical and adult-use customers, with separate menus and dedicated service areas for each to ensure a smooth experience for all shoppers.

All from trusted brands known for quality and consistency.

Can I order online and pick up in-store?
Yes! You can browse menus and place orders online for in-store pickup at all Sunnyside IL locations. It’s a quick and easy way to secure your favorite products.
Are there daily deals or specials?
Yes — we offer daily savings, product spotlights, and exclusive promotions that rotate regularly. Check your local store page or visit in-store to see what’s available.

Where are Sunnyside dispensaries located in Illinois?

Concentrates offer all the enjoyable aspects of cannabis, without having to burn the plant.

Edibles are the ideal smoke-free alternative for anyone from beginners to more experienced users. Infused gummies, snacks or drinks make incorporating cannabis into an active lifestyle and wellness routine simple. Keep in mind, eating cannabis offers a different experience than smoking or vaping.

What does 420 mean?
The term “420” was coined in the 1970s by a group of five friends from San Rafael, CA who would regularly meet up at 4:20pm to smoke cannabis. As it wasn’t yet legal, “420” became their code word.
420 Catches On

4:20pm soon became that go-to time to start a session with friends. “420-friendly” came to mean that a group, place or event was open to adult-use cannabis and April 20th, since it falls on 4/20, has become the unofficial holiday to celebrate cannabis.

data.text: April 20: A Day for Change

As cannabis legalization has gained steam over the years, April 20th has given rise to growing rallies, trade shows, and concerts—all to advocate for legislation, normalize its use, and celebrate cannabis culture.
420 For All

Nowadays 4/20 is open to the masses, as cannabis use gains acceptance in the mainstream. What started off with a cult-following has expanded to a world where ultimately everyone is free to feel like cannabis can be right for them.
